# Introduction

This analysis examines long-term temperature changes and
daily weather prediction through three applications of
latent-state time series models.

*First*, we analyze monthly Northern Hemisphere temperature
anomalies from GISTEMP over 1880–2025. After exploring the
series and removing its residual seasonal component, we fit
Gaussian Hidden Markov Models with different numbers of
states. Information criteria guide model selection, and
Viterbi decoding describes the sequence of latent states.
We assess whether these states provide a useful summary
of long-term changes and discuss the limitations of
representing gradual warming through discrete levels.

*Second*, we analyze the same seasonally adjusted series using
a random walk plus noise model and a local linear trend
model. Variance parameters are estimated by maximum
likelihood, and Kalman filtering and smoothing reconstruct
the latent temperature level. Ten-year changes in the
smoothed level describe how the magnitude of warming varies
across the record. We distinguish these changes from the
LLT slope and compare the continuous-valued representation
with the discrete states of the HMM.

*Third*, we examine daily maximum temperatures at Houlton AP
and Augusta State AP using GHCN observations. The analysis
covers January 1988–December 2024, a complete daily period
for both stations that avoids a prolonged gap in the earlier
Houlton record. After removing the annual seasonal pattern,
we fit three bivariate Dynamic Linear Models: independent
state innovations, unrestricted innovation covariance, and
distance-based covariance. We compare their fit,
interpretability, and in-sample one-step-ahead prediction
errors to assess the contribution of cross-station dependence.

The GISTEMP analysis provides a retrospective description
of temperature dynamics. The weather predictions are
evaluated with parameters and seasonal adjustment estimated
on the same sample, so their comparison does not establish
out-of-sample forecasting performance.

# Temperature Anomalies and Seasonal Adjustment

The analysis uses the GISTEMP record of monthly Northern
Hemisphere temperature anomalies, measured in degrees Celsius
relative to the calendar-month averages for 1951–1980.
We extract the monthly columns from the supplied dataset,
obtaining a complete series of 1,752 observations from
January 1880 to December 2025 that requires no interpolation.

```{r load-gistemp}
gistemp_path <- "data/gistemp.csv"

if (!file.exists(gistemp_path)) {
  gistemp_path <- paste0(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
    "MnGianmaria/Time-series-analysis/main/",
    "07_climate_and_weather_models/data/gistemp.csv"
  )
}

gistemp_raw <- read.csv(
  gistemp_path,
  skip = 1,
  na.strings = "***",
  check.names = FALSE
)

month_names <- c(
  "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
  "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"
)

monthly_values <- as.numeric(
  t(as.matrix(gistemp_raw[, month_names]))
)

stopifnot(
  identical(as.integer(gistemp_raw$Year), 1880:2025),
  length(monthly_values) == 1752,
  all(is.finite(monthly_values))
)

gistemp_ts <- ts(
  monthly_values,
  start = c(1880, 1),
  frequency = 12
)

gistemp_data <- data.frame(
  Date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(gistemp_ts))),
  Temperature = as.numeric(gistemp_ts)
)
```

To separate the long-term movement from residual seasonality,
we apply additive STL decomposition with a periodic seasonal
window and subtract the estimated seasonal component.
Since the observations are already anomalies relative to
calendar-month averages, this adjustment concerns the seasonal
pattern remaining in the anomaly series. The periodic
specification holds that pattern fixed across years, with
estimation based on the full record for this retrospective
analysis.

```{r gistemp-seasonal-adjustment}
gistemp_stl <- stl(
  gistemp_ts,
  s.window = "periodic"
)

gistemp_adj <- gistemp_ts -
  gistemp_stl$time.series[, "seasonal"]

climate_data <- data.frame(
  Date = gistemp_data$Date,
  Time = as.numeric(time(gistemp_adj)),
  Temperature = as.numeric(gistemp_adj)
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(climate_data) == length(gistemp_ts),
  all(is.finite(climate_data$Temperature))
)
```

```{r gistemp-exploratory-plots, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=4.2, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Exploratory analysis of GISTEMP monthly anomalies. Panel A groups the original observations by calendar month; panels B and C show their sample ACF and PACF, with lags in months and approximate white-noise reference bounds. Panel D shows the seasonally adjusted series."}
climate_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 9,
      face = "bold",
      hjust = 0
    ),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )

month_data <- gistemp_data
month_data$Month <- factor(
  cycle(gistemp_ts),
  levels = 1:12,
  labels = month.abb
)

p_month <- ggplot(
  month_data,
  aes(x = Month, y = Temperature)
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    color = "#243746",
    fill = "#EDF1F5",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    outlier.size = 0.4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "A  Distribution by month",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  climate_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))

acf_result <- acf(
  as.numeric(gistemp_ts),
  lag.max = 48,
  plot = FALSE
)

pacf_result <- pacf(
  as.numeric(gistemp_ts),
  lag.max = 48,
  plot = FALSE
)

acf_data <- data.frame(
  Lag = as.numeric(acf_result$lag)[-1],
  Correlation = as.numeric(acf_result$acf)[-1]
)

pacf_data <- data.frame(
  Lag = as.numeric(pacf_result$lag),
  Correlation = as.numeric(pacf_result$acf)
)

reference_bound <- qnorm(0.975) /
  sqrt(length(gistemp_ts))

correlation_plot <- function(data, title, y_label) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = Lag, y = Correlation)) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = 0,
      color = "grey60",
      linewidth = 0.3
    ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = c(-reference_bound, reference_bound),
      color = "#B36B35",
      linetype = "dashed",
      linewidth = 0.3
    ) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(xend = Lag, yend = 0),
      color = "#24476B",
      linewidth = 0.35
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = seq(0, 48, 12)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Lag (months)",
      y = y_label
    ) +
    climate_theme
}

p_acf <- correlation_plot(
  acf_data,
  "B  Autocorrelation",
  "ACF"
)

p_pacf <- correlation_plot(
  pacf_data,
  "C  Partial autocorrelation",
  "PACF"
)

p_adjusted <- ggplot(
  climate_data,
  aes(x = Date, y = Temperature)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "grey60",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#24476B",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(
      paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 40), "-01-01")
    ),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "D  Seasonally adjusted series",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  climate_theme

(p_month | p_acf) / (p_pacf | p_adjusted)
```
The monthly distributions have similar medians, although
dispersion is greater in the winter months, so the boxplots
do not suggest a pronounced seasonal pattern in the central
level of the anomalies. Temporal dependence is substantial:
the ACF remains strongly positive through 48 months, while
the PACF is dominated by the first lag but retains smaller
positive values over several subsequent lags. Because these
correlations are calculated on a series with a changing
level, they should not be read as identifying a stationary
autoregressive specification.

The seasonally adjusted series places these patterns in
context, showing predominantly negative anomalies early in
the record and a sustained rise in recent decades alongside
considerable monthly variation. This motivates models that
allow the underlying level to evolve, while leaving open
whether discrete states or a continuous-valued latent process
provide the more useful description.

```{r gistemp-stl-plot, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=4.2, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Additive STL decomposition of Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies. All components are expressed in degrees Celsius, with separate vertical scales. The seasonal pattern is fixed across years by the periodic specification."}
stl_components <- data.frame(
  Date = gistemp_data$Date,
  Observed = as.numeric(gistemp_ts),
  Trend = as.numeric(gistemp_stl$time.series[, "trend"]),
  Seasonal = as.numeric(gistemp_stl$time.series[, "seasonal"]),
  Remainder = as.numeric(gistemp_stl$time.series[, "remainder"])
)

stl_long <- pivot_longer(
  stl_components,
  cols = -Date,
  names_to = "Component",
  values_to = "Value"
)

stl_long$Component <- factor(
  stl_long$Component,
  levels = c("Observed", "Trend", "Seasonal", "Remainder")
)

ggplot(stl_long, aes(x = Date, y = Value)) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#243746",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~Component,
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(
      paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")
    ),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 3)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Anomaly component (°C)"
  ) +
  climate_theme +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#F2F2F2",
      color = NA
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(
      size = 8,
      hjust = 0
    ),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.6, "lines")
  )
```

The STL trend shows an increase from the early twentieth
century to the 1940s, followed by a period of relatively
stable levels and a sustained rise from around the 1970s.
This movement is much larger than the estimated seasonal
component, whose deviations remain within a few hundredths
of a degree. The repetition of that seasonal pattern follows
from the periodic specification and should not be interpreted
as independent evidence that seasonality is constant.

The remainder fluctuates around zero without the sustained
upward movement visible in the observed series, although
several large deviations remain. STL provides a descriptive
separation of these components; the following models examine
how the changing level can be represented through latent
states and how ten-year changes vary across the record.

With a trend smoothing window of
`r unname(gistemp_stl$win["t"])` months, the STL trend
component retains interannual movements and should not
be interpreted as a trend restricted to climatic time scales.

# Hidden Markov Models

We model the seasonally adjusted anomalies as observations
from a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model, in which an unobserved
state \(S_t \in \{1,\ldots,K\}\) determines the mean and
variance of the temperature distribution:

\[
y_t \mid S_t=j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_j,\sigma_j^2),
\qquad
\Pr(S_t=j\mid S_{t-1}=i)=p_{ij}.
\]

The state sequence follows a first-order Markov chain with
constant transition probabilities, and observations are
assumed independent conditional on that sequence. This
specification can summarize persistent differences in
temperature levels without fixing the dates of transitions
in advance, although gradual changes may be represented
through switches between states.

We estimate models with two through five states by maximum
likelihood using the EM algorithm. Each specification is
fitted from 25 random initializations, retaining the converged
solution with the highest likelihood. BIC is the primary
selection criterion, while AIC is reported for comparison;
multiple starts reduce sensitivity to initialization without
guaranteeing a global maximum.

All 25 initializations converged for each specification.
For the selected five-state model, 23 reached a log-likelihood
within \(10^{-4}\) of the best retained value, whereas
the best four-state solution was reached only once,
indicating greater sensitivity to initialization for
that specification.

```{r fit-climate-hmm, cache=TRUE, results='hide'}
candidate_states <- 2:5
hmm_seeds <- 123:147

fit_hmm_starts <- function(k, data, seeds) {
  best_model <- NULL
  best_loglik <- -Inf

  attempts <- data.frame(
    Seed = seeds,
    LogLik = NA_real_,
    Converged = FALSE,
    Status = NA_character_
  )

  for (i in seq_along(seeds)) {
    set.seed(seeds[i])

    current_fit <- tryCatch(
      {
        model <- depmix(
          Temperature ~ 1,
          data = data,
          nstates = k,
          family = gaussian()
        )

        fit(
          model,
          verbose = FALSE,
          emcontrol = em.control(
            maxit = 2000,
            tol = 1e-8,
            random.start = TRUE
          )
        )
      },
      error = function(e) e
    )

    if (inherits(current_fit, "error")) {
      attempts$Status[i] <- conditionMessage(current_fit)
      next
    }

    current_loglik <- as.numeric(logLik(current_fit))
    current_status <- paste(
      current_fit@message,
      collapse = " "
    )

    converged <- is.finite(current_loglik) &&
      grepl(
        "^Log likelihood converged",
        trimws(current_status),
        ignore.case = TRUE
      )

    attempts$LogLik[i] <- current_loglik
    attempts$Converged[i] <- converged
    attempts$Status[i] <- current_status

    if (converged && current_loglik > best_loglik) {
      best_model <- current_fit
      best_loglik <- current_loglik
    }
  }

  if (is.null(best_model)) {
    stop("No converged HMM obtained for K = ", k)
  }

  list(
    model = best_model,
    attempts = attempts
  )
}

hmm_runs <- lapply(
  candidate_states,
  function(k) {
    fit_hmm_starts(k, climate_data, hmm_seeds)
  }
)

names(hmm_runs) <- as.character(candidate_states)

hmm_models <- lapply(hmm_runs, function(x) x$model)

hmm_comparison <- data.frame(
  States = candidate_states,
  LogLik = vapply(
    hmm_models,
    function(model) as.numeric(logLik(model)),
    numeric(1)
  ),
  AIC = vapply(hmm_models, AIC, numeric(1)),
  BIC = vapply(hmm_models, BIC, numeric(1))
)

rownames(hmm_comparison) <- NULL

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(hmm_comparison)))
)

best_hmm_k <- hmm_comparison$States[
  which.min(hmm_comparison$BIC)
]

best_hmm_fit <- hmm_models[[as.character(best_hmm_k)]]
```

```{r hmm-selection-table, results='asis'}
kable(
  hmm_comparison,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("States", "Log-likelihood", "AIC", "BIC"),
  caption = "Gaussian HMM comparison, retaining the highest-likelihood converged solution from 25 initializations per specification."
)
```

Both AIC and BIC decrease throughout the candidate range,
with their lowest values attained by the five-state model.
Following the BIC selection rule, we retain this specification
for parameter interpretation and decoding. Since the minimum
occurs at the upper limit of the explored range, the comparison
does not establish that five states would remain preferable
if more states were considered.

The improvement in fit indicates that additional states help
represent the changing distribution of temperature anomalies,
but it does not establish the existence of five distinct
physical climate regimes. In a series with a sustained trend,
a level-based HMM may use successive states to approximate
gradual movement.

For interpretation, states are ordered by increasing estimated
mean anomaly. The response parameters describe the Gaussian
distribution associated with each state, while the transition
matrix reports the probabilities estimated by the HMM.
These probabilities differ from transition frequencies
calculated by counting switches in a decoded sequence.

```{r extract-hmm-parameters}
response_parameters <- lapply(
  seq_len(best_hmm_k),
  function(j) {
    getpars(
      getmodel(
        best_hmm_fit,
        which = "response",
        state = j,
        number = 1
      )
    )
  }
)

stopifnot(
  all(lengths(response_parameters) == 2)
)

hmm_means_raw <- vapply(
  response_parameters,
  function(x) x[1],
  numeric(1)
)

hmm_sds_raw <- vapply(
  response_parameters,
  function(x) x[2],
  numeric(1)
)

transition_rows <- lapply(
  seq_len(best_hmm_k),
  function(j) {
    getpars(
      getmodel(
        best_hmm_fit,
        which = "transition",
        state = j
      )
    )
  }
)

stopifnot(
  all(lengths(transition_rows) == best_hmm_k)
)

transition_raw <- do.call(rbind, transition_rows)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(hmm_means_raw)),
  all(is.finite(hmm_sds_raw)),
  all(hmm_sds_raw > 0),
  all(is.finite(transition_raw)),
  all(transition_raw >= -1e-8),
  all(transition_raw <= 1 + 1e-8),
  all(abs(rowSums(transition_raw) - 1) < 1e-8)
)

hmm_state_order <- order(hmm_means_raw)

hmm_means <- hmm_means_raw[hmm_state_order]
hmm_sds <- hmm_sds_raw[hmm_state_order]

hmm_transition <- transition_raw[
  hmm_state_order,
  hmm_state_order,
  drop = FALSE
]

hmm_labels <- paste("State", seq_len(best_hmm_k))

hmm_parameters <- data.frame(
  State = hmm_labels,
  Mean = hmm_means,
  SD = hmm_sds
)

transition_display <- data.frame(
  From = hmm_labels,
  hmm_transition,
  check.names = FALSE
)

names(transition_display) <- c(
  "From / To",
  hmm_labels
)
```

```{r hmm-response-table, results='asis'}
kable(
  hmm_parameters,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "State",
    "Mean anomaly (°C)",
    "SD (°C)"
  ),
  caption = "Estimated Gaussian response parameters, with states ordered by increasing mean anomaly."
)
```

```{r hmm-transition-table, results='asis'}
kable(
  transition_display,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Estimated HMM transition probabilities. Rows identify the current state and columns the following state, using the same ordering as the response-parameter table."
)
```

The estimated state means range from -0.449 °C to 1.288 °C,
with the two lowest states below the reference-period average
and the remaining three above it. Dispersion also differs
across states: State 2 has the smallest estimated standard
deviation, while State 5 has the largest, so the classification
reflects differences in both level and variability.

Self-transition probabilities are high, ranging from about
0.900 to a value reported as 1.000 for State 5. For States
1–4, the fitted probabilities imply expected durations of
roughly 10–39 months, rather than uniformly long-lasting
regimes. The near-boundary estimate for State 5 requires
particular caution: it describes persistence within this
fitted sample and should not be interpreted as evidence
that the highest-temperature state is permanently absorbing.
The decoded sequence will show where these states occur
and whether they recur across the record.

We recover the most likely joint state sequence using Viterbi
decoding and plot the observations alongside the estimated
mean of their assigned state. Decoding uses the full sample,
so the resulting classification is retrospective rather than
a reconstruction of what could have been identified in real time.

```{r decode-climate-hmm}
hmm_states_raw <- posterior(
  best_hmm_fit,
  type = "viterbi"
)$state

state_mapping <- integer(best_hmm_k)
state_mapping[hmm_state_order] <- seq_len(best_hmm_k)

hmm_states <- state_mapping[hmm_states_raw]

stopifnot(
  length(hmm_states) == nrow(climate_data),
  all(hmm_states %in% seq_len(best_hmm_k))
)

hmm_decoded <- climate_data

hmm_decoded$State <- factor(
  hmm_states,
  levels = seq_len(best_hmm_k),
  labels = hmm_labels
)

hmm_decoded$StateMean <- hmm_means[hmm_states]
```

```{r hmm-decoded-plot, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Viterbi-decoded states of the selected Gaussian HMM. Points show seasonally adjusted anomalies coloured by assigned state; the black step line shows the corresponding estimated state mean. State labels follow increasing mean anomaly."}
state_colors <- setNames(
  c(
    "#24476B",
    "#508C95",
    "#63876B",
    "#B36B35",
    "#914B59"
  )[seq_len(best_hmm_k)],
  hmm_labels
)

ggplot(hmm_decoded, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "grey60",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Temperature),
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = Temperature, color = State),
    size = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_step(
    aes(y = StateMean),
    color = "#222222",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = state_colors,
    drop = FALSE,
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(
      paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")
    ),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  climate_theme +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(0.8, "lines")
  )
```

The decoded sequence assigns most early observations to the
three lower-mean states, with repeated switches rather than
a small number of permanent transitions. More sustained
assignments to the higher states emerge later in the record:
State 4 dominates from the late 1990s to the mid-2010s,
after which State 5 persists through the end of the sample.
These transitions summarize the shift towards higher
temperature anomalies, but their dates depend on the fitted
specification and do not independently establish physical
climate change points.

The HMM provides a useful classification of temperature
levels, while its stepwise representation approximates
movement that need not occur through abrupt changes.
The final uninterrupted assignment to State 5 extends
to the sample endpoint, so the duration of that final
visit is only partially observed. Its near-boundary
persistence estimate should therefore not be interpreted
as evidence of permanent absorption. Conditional independence
given the state sequence remains restrictive, and residual
serial dependence has not been assessed here.

# Dynamic Linear Models and Decadal Changes

We now represent temperature anomalies through a continuous-valued
latent level, comparing a random walk plus noise model (RW)
with a local linear trend model (LLT). In the RW specification,
the level evolves through random innovations:

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \mu_t + \varepsilon_t,
& \varepsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),\\
\mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \eta_t,
& \eta_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2).
\end{aligned}
\]

The LLT specification introduces a slope that can itself
change over time:

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \mu_t + \varepsilon_t,
& \varepsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),\\
\mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + \eta_t,
& \eta_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2),\\
\beta_t &= \beta_{t-1} + \zeta_t,
& \zeta_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\gamma^2).
\end{aligned}
\]

Here \(\mu_t\) is the latent anomaly level in degrees Celsius
and \(\beta_t\) is the slope in degrees Celsius per month.
Observation errors and state innovations are mutually
independent, independent over time, and independent of the
initial state. Both specifications allow stochastic level
changes, while LLT additionally permits slope changes;
a slope innovation variance near zero would indicate little
variation in the slope, without implying that the slope
itself is zero.

We estimate the variance parameters by maximum likelihood
on the full adjusted record, using logarithmic parameters
to ensure positivity and Gaussian initial distributions
with zero means and covariance \(10^7 I\) as a diffuse
approximation. Approximate standard errors are obtained
from the numerical Hessian through the delta method when
its conditioning permits inversion. The slope-variance
standard error is omitted if the estimate is numerically
near the boundary.

```{r fit-climate-dlm, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=as.numeric(gistemp_adj)}
build_rw <- function(log_variances) {
  dlmModPoly(
    order = 1,
    dV = exp(log_variances[1]),
    dW = exp(log_variances[2]),
    m0 = 0,
    C0 = matrix(1e7, 1, 1)
  )
}

build_llt <- function(log_variances) {
  dlmModPoly(
    order = 2,
    dV = exp(log_variances[1]),
    dW = exp(log_variances[2:3]),
    m0 = c(0, 0),
    C0 = diag(1e7, 2)
  )
}

sample_variance <- var(as.numeric(gistemp_adj))

fit_rw <- dlmMLE(
  gistemp_adj,
  parm = log(c(sample_variance, sample_variance / 10)),
  build = build_rw,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 2000, reltol = 1e-10)
)

fit_llt <- dlmMLE(
  gistemp_adj,
  parm = log(c(
    sample_variance,
    sample_variance / 10,
    sample_variance / 100
  )),
  build = build_llt,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 2000, reltol = 1e-10)
)

stopifnot(
  fit_rw$convergence == 0,
  fit_llt$convergence == 0,
  all(is.finite(fit_rw$par)),
  all(is.finite(fit_llt$par))
)

mod_rw <- build_rw(fit_rw$par)
mod_llt <- build_llt(fit_llt$par)

variance_standard_errors <- function(fit) {
  estimates <- exp(fit$par)
  unavailable <- rep(NA_real_, length(estimates))

  H <- (fit$hessian + t(fit$hessian)) / 2

  if (any(!is.finite(H))) {
    return(unavailable)
  }

  eigenvalues <- eigen(H, symmetric = TRUE)$values

  if (min(eigenvalues) <= 1e-8 * max(abs(eigenvalues))) {
    return(unavailable)
  }

  estimates * sqrt(diag(solve(H)))
}

rw_estimates <- exp(fit_rw$par)
llt_estimates <- exp(fit_llt$par)

dlm_variances <- data.frame(
  Model = c("RW", "RW", "LLT", "LLT", "LLT"),
  Parameter = c(
    "Observation variance",
    "Level innovation variance",
    "Observation variance",
    "Level innovation variance",
    "Slope innovation variance"
  ),
  Estimate = c(rw_estimates, llt_estimates),
  SE = c(
    variance_standard_errors(fit_rw),
    variance_standard_errors(fit_llt)
  )
)
```

```{r climate-dlm-variance-table, results='asis'}
dlm_variance_display <- dlm_variances

dlm_variance_display$Estimate <- formatC(
  dlm_variances$Estimate,
  format = "e",
  digits = 3
)

dlm_variance_display$SE <- ifelse(
  is.na(dlm_variances$SE),
  "Unavailable",
  formatC(dlm_variances$SE, format = "e", digits = 3)
)

slope_near_boundary <-
  llt_estimates[3] / llt_estimates[1] < 1e-6

if (slope_near_boundary) {
  dlm_variance_display$Estimate[5] <- "Near zero"
  dlm_variance_display$SE[5] <- "Not reported"
}

kable(
  dlm_variance_display,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "Model", "Parameter", "Estimate", "Approx. SE"
  ),
  caption = "Full-sample maximum-likelihood variance estimates. Approximate standard errors use the numerical Hessian and delta method. The slope-variance standard error is omitted because the estimate is numerically near zero; the remaining LLT standard errors are local approximations from the full Hessian and require caution near this boundary."
)
```
The two specifications yield similar observation variances,
approximately `r sprintf("%.4f", rw_estimates[1])` for RW,
and level innovation variances, approximately
`r sprintf("%.4f", rw_estimates[2])`. Their ratio in the RW
model is `r sprintf("%.2f", rw_estimates[2] / rw_estimates[1])`.
The reconstructed level follows sustained movements while
reducing some monthly noise, but retains considerable
interannual variability; it should therefore not be
interpreted as an isolated long-term climate trend.

The LLT slope innovation variance is numerically near zero,
making the fitted model approximately a random walk with
constant drift. The drift can be nonzero, while level
innovations allow departures from that constant-drift
evolution. A near-boundary variance estimate does not,
by itself, establish that the underlying pace of warming
is constant, since the allocation of variation between
level and slope depends on the model specification.
The slope-variance standard error is omitted because
the usual normal approximation is unreliable near
the boundary.

Kalman filtering estimates the latent level using observations
up to each month, while smoothing also incorporates subsequent
observations. We compare both reconstructions with the adjusted
series and report pointwise 95 percent intervals for the
smoothed latent level, conditional on the estimated parameters
and seasonal adjustment. These are state uncertainty intervals,
not prediction intervals for observations, so observations
outside the bands do not by themselves indicate poor coverage.
Since parameters and seasonal adjustment are estimated from
the full record, the comparison remains retrospective even
for the filtered estimates.

```{r climate-filtering-smoothing}
filter_rw <- dlmFilter(gistemp_adj, mod_rw)
filter_llt <- dlmFilter(gistemp_adj, mod_llt)

smooth_rw <- dlmSmooth(filter_rw)
smooth_llt <- dlmSmooth(filter_llt)

extract_climate_levels <- function(filtered, smoothed, model_name) {
  filtered_mean <- as.matrix(filtered$m)[-1, 1]
  smoothed_mean <- as.matrix(smoothed$s)[-1, 1]

  filtered_cov <- dlmSvd2var(
    filtered$U.C,
    filtered$D.C
  )

  smoothed_cov <- dlmSvd2var(
    smoothed$U.S,
    smoothed$D.S
  )

  filtered_variance <- vapply(
    filtered_cov[-1],
    function(x) as.numeric(x[1, 1]),
    numeric(1)
  )

  smoothed_variance <- vapply(
    smoothed_cov[-1],
    function(x) as.numeric(x[1, 1]),
    numeric(1)
  )

  stopifnot(
    length(filtered_mean) == nrow(climate_data),
    length(smoothed_mean) == nrow(climate_data),
    all(is.finite(filtered_mean)),
    all(is.finite(smoothed_mean)),
    all(is.finite(filtered_variance)),
    all(is.finite(smoothed_variance)),
    all(filtered_variance >= 0),
    all(smoothed_variance >= 0),
    all(smoothed_variance <= filtered_variance + 1e-6),
    isTRUE(all.equal(
      tail(filtered_mean, 1),
      tail(smoothed_mean, 1)
    ))
  )

  data.frame(
    Date = climate_data$Date,
    Observed = climate_data$Temperature,
    Filtered = filtered_mean,
    Smoothed = smoothed_mean,
    Lower = smoothed_mean -
      qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(smoothed_variance),
    Upper = smoothed_mean +
      qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(smoothed_variance),
    Model = model_name
  )
}

climate_levels_rw <- extract_climate_levels(
  filter_rw, smooth_rw, "RW"
)

climate_levels_llt <- extract_climate_levels(
  filter_llt, smooth_llt, "LLT"
)

climate_levels <- rbind(
  climate_levels_rw,
  climate_levels_llt
)

climate_levels$Model <- factor(
  climate_levels$Model,
  levels = c("RW", "LLT")
)
```

```{r climate-dlm-levels-plot, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=2.5, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Filtered and smoothed latent levels under RW and LLT. Shaded bands show pointwise 95 percent conditional smoothing intervals for the latent level, excluding parameter and seasonal-adjustment uncertainty. Both panels use the same axes."}
ggplot(climate_levels, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper),
    fill = "#24476B",
    alpha = 0.18,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Observed, color = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Filtered, color = "Filtered"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Smoothed, color = "Smoothed"),
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~Model, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "#BBBBBB",
      "Filtered" = "#B36B35",
      "Smoothed" = "#24476B"
    ),
    breaks = c("Observed", "Filtered", "Smoothed"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        linetype = c("solid", "dashed", "solid"),
        linewidth = c(0.4, 0.5, 0.5)
      )
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(
      paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")
    ),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  climate_theme +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#F2F2F2",
      color = NA
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.5, "lines"),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.8, "lines")
  )
```
RW and LLT produce nearly indistinguishable level
reconstructions at this plotting scale, both capturing
the sustained rise in recent decades while attenuating
monthly fluctuations. The filtered and smoothed estimates
follow similar trajectories, although smoothing revises
local movements using subsequent observations. The visual
similarity between the models is consistent with their
similar estimated observation and level innovation variances,
but does not establish equivalence or equal predictive ability.

To describe the pace of warming over successive ten-year
windows, we calculate the difference between the smoothed
LLT level and its value 120 months earlier:

\[
\Delta_{10,t}
=
\hat{\mu}_{t\mid T}
-
\hat{\mu}_{t-120\mid T}.
\]

This quantity measures the net change over the preceding
ten years and can be interpreted as an average warming rate
over that window, expressed in degrees Celsius per decade.
It differs from the LLT slope component because changes
in the latent level also accumulate through level innovations.
We compare it with the smoothed monthly slope multiplied
by 120, using the same fitted model throughout.

```{r climate-decadal-changes}
smoothed_slope <- as.matrix(smooth_llt$s)[-1, 2]
smoothed_level <- climate_levels_llt$Smoothed
n_months <- length(smoothed_level)

stopifnot(
  n_months > 120,
  length(smoothed_slope) == n_months,
  all(is.finite(smoothed_slope))
)

climate_decadal <- data.frame(
  Date = climate_levels_llt$Date,
  DecadalChange = c(
    rep(NA_real_, 120),
    smoothed_level[121:n_months] -
      smoothed_level[1:(n_months - 120)]
  ),
  SlopePerDecade = 120 * smoothed_slope
)

climate_decadal_long <- climate_decadal |>
  filter(is.finite(DecadalChange)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(DecadalChange, SlopePerDecade),
    names_to = "Series",
    values_to = "Rate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Series = factor(
      Series,
      levels = c("DecadalChange", "SlopePerDecade"),
      labels = c(
        "Ten-year level change",
        "LLT slope (per decade)"
      )
    )
  )
```

```{r climate-decadal-changes-plot, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Ten-year backward changes in the smoothed LLT level, compared with the smoothed monthly slope multiplied by 120. Both quantities use the model fitted to the seasonally adjusted series. The ten-year change summarizes movement over an overlapping window; it is not an instantaneous slope estimate or a formal test of acceleration."}
ggplot(
  climate_decadal_long,
  aes(
    x = Date,
    y = Rate,
    color = Series,
    linetype = Series
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#888888",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Ten-year level change" = "#B36B35",
      "LLT slope (per decade)" = "#24476B"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "Ten-year level change" = "solid",
      "LLT slope (per decade)" = "dashed"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(
      paste0(seq(1900, 2020, 20), "-01-01")
    ),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Warming rate (°C per decade)"
  ) +
  climate_theme +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.5, "lines")
  )
```

The ten-year changes alternate between positive and negative
values from the 1890s through the 1970s. From around 1980,
positive changes become more prevalent, although substantial
fluctuations remain and the measure falls sharply at the
end of the sample. Because each difference compares two
monthly smoothed levels ten years apart, it remains sensitive
to interannual variability at both endpoints; a fall in
this measure does not necessarily imply a decline in
the temperature level.

The final ten-year change is only
`r sprintf("%.3f", tail(climate_decadal$DecadalChange, 1))` °C,
because the smoothed levels in December 2015 and December
2025 are nearly equal. This illustrates the sensitivity
of the measure to its endpoints: it does not imply that
temperatures remained constant throughout the intervening
decade.

The nearly constant LLT slope provides a sample-wide
reference, while departures from it in the ten-year changes
reflect accumulated level innovations. The figure therefore
describes variation in average temperature changes across
overlapping windows, without separating long-term changes
in warming from shorter-term variability. The uncertainty
of these differences has not been quantified.

Compared with the HMM, the DLMs provide a more natural
representation of gradual movements through an evolving
numerical level, whereas the HMM offers an interpretable
classification into a few temperature states, with repeated
switches among them during parts of the record. Both
frameworks use a latent Markov process, conditionally
independent observations, maximum-likelihood estimation,
and filtering and smoothing recursions. For a Gaussian DLM, the joint conditional mode coincides
with the conditional mean, whose components are the marginal
smoothed means. HMM Viterbi decoding instead selects the
most likely joint discrete sequence, which can differ from
the sequence of marginally most probable states obtained
from forward-backward smoothing. The Viterbi path alone
does not display classification uncertainty, although
the HMM can provide smoothed state probabilities; the
Gaussian smoother provides state means and variances.
The comparison here concerns representation of the observed
record, since predictive performance is not compared
between the frameworks.

# Weather Station Data and Seasonal Adjustment

We now turn from monthly hemispheric anomalies to daily
maximum temperatures at Houlton AP and Augusta State AP
in Maine, using the station pair suggested in the assignment.
The aim is to examine whether allowing dependence between
their latent temperature levels improves the fit and
one-step-ahead predictions relative to modelling the stations
independently.

Although both records extend from June 1948 to December 2024,
Houlton has a continuous gap of 944 days from May 1, 1985
to November 30, 1987. We begin the analysis in January 1988,
the first complete calendar year after this gap, and retain
observations through December 2024. The resulting common
period contains 13,515 consecutive daily observations at
each station, including leap days. This choice excludes
valid earlier observations in exchange for a continuous,
aligned sample, without interpolating missing temperatures
or compressing the time axis. It is based on data availability
rather than model performance. Maximum temperatures are
converted from tenths of a degree Celsius to degrees Celsius
before the analysis.

```{r load-weather-data}
weather_path <- "data/ghcn_maine.csv"

if (!file.exists(weather_path)) {
  weather_path <- paste0(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
    "MnGianmaria/Time-series-analysis/main/",
    "07_climate_and_weather_models/data/ghcn_maine.csv"
  )
}

weather_raw <- read.csv(
  weather_path,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

stopifnot(
  all(
    c(
      "ID", "station", "latitude", "longitude",
      "elevation", "date", "TMAX"
    ) %in% names(weather_raw)
  )
)

weather_raw$date <- as.Date(weather_raw$date)

station_ids <- c(
  "Houlton AP" = "USW00014609",
  "Augusta State AP" = "USW00014605"
)

weather_start <- as.Date("1988-01-01")
weather_end <- as.Date("2024-12-31")

weather_dates <- seq(
  weather_start,
  weather_end,
  by = "day"
)

weather_data <- weather_raw |>
  filter(
    ID %in% unname(station_ids),
    date >= weather_start,
    date <= weather_end
  ) |>
  transmute(
    ID,
    Station = factor(
      ID,
      levels = unname(station_ids),
      labels = names(station_ids)
    ),
    Date = date,
    Latitude = latitude,
    Longitude = longitude,
    Elevation = elevation,
    Temperature = TMAX / 10
  ) |>
  arrange(Station, Date)

stopifnot(
  length(weather_dates) == 13515L,
  nrow(weather_data) == 2L * length(weather_dates),
  !anyDuplicated(weather_data[c("ID", "Date")]),
  all(is.finite(weather_data$Temperature)),
  all(weather_data$Temperature != -999.9)
)

for (station_id in unname(station_ids)) {
  station_dates <- sort(
    weather_data$Date[weather_data$ID == station_id]
  )

  missing_dates <- weather_dates[
    !weather_dates %in% station_dates
  ]

  extra_dates <- station_dates[
    !station_dates %in% weather_dates
  ]

  if (
    length(station_dates) != length(weather_dates) ||
    length(missing_dates) > 0L ||
    length(extra_dates) > 0L
  ) {
    stop(
      "Calendar check failed for ", station_id,
      "\nObserved days: ", length(station_dates),
      "\nExpected days: ", length(weather_dates),
      "\nFirst missing dates: ",
      paste(head(missing_dates), collapse = ", "),
      "\nFirst unexpected dates: ",
      paste(head(extra_dates), collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  stopifnot(
    identical(
      as.numeric(station_dates),
      as.numeric(weather_dates)
    )
  )
}
weather_station_summary <- weather_data |>
  group_by(Station) |>
  summarise(
    Latitude = first(Latitude),
    Longitude = first(Longitude),
    `Elevation (m)` = first(Elevation),
    Days = n(),
    Start = as.character(min(Date)),
    End = as.character(max(Date)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```
```{r weather-station-table, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  weather_station_summary,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  row.names = FALSE,
  digits = c(0, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  caption = paste(
    "Selected weather stations and analysis period.",
    "Daily maximum temperatures are available on every",
    "calendar day of the selected period at both stations."
  )
)
```
We remove the annual seasonal pattern separately for each
station using additive STL with a periodic seasonal window.
To keep the seasonal cycle aligned with calendar dates,
STL is fitted to a 365-day calendar excluding February 29.
The resulting seasonal pattern is then mapped back to the
complete daily record, assigning February 29 the average
of the seasonal components for February 28 and March 1.
Only the seasonal component is interpolated in this step;
all observed temperatures, including those on leap days,
are retained for subsequent modelling.

Subtracting this fixed seasonal pattern leaves a series
containing the temperature level, its longer-term movements,
and daily fluctuations. Seasonal adjustment uses the full
1988–2024 sample, so the subsequent one-step predictions
are evaluated within a retrospective analysis rather than
as forecasts based exclusively on information available
at the time.
```{r weather-seasonal-adjustment}
adjust_weather_station <- function(station_data) {
  station_data <- station_data[
    order(station_data$Date),
  ]

  month_day <- format(station_data$Date, "%m-%d")
  non_leap_day <- month_day != "02-29"

  seasonal_fit <- stats::stl(
    ts(
      station_data$Temperature[non_leap_day],
      start = c(1988, 1),
      frequency = 365
    ),
    s.window = "periodic"
  )

  reference_days <- format(
    seq(
      as.Date("2001-01-01"),
      as.Date("2001-12-31"),
      by = "day"
    ),
    "%m-%d"
  )

  seasonal_pattern <- tapply(
    as.numeric(
      seasonal_fit$time.series[, "seasonal"]
    ),
    factor(
      month_day[non_leap_day],
      levels = reference_days
    ),
    mean
  )

  seasonal_pattern <- setNames(
    as.numeric(seasonal_pattern),
    reference_days
  )

  seasonal_component <- unname(
    seasonal_pattern[month_day]
  )

  seasonal_component[!non_leap_day] <- mean(
    seasonal_pattern[c("02-28", "03-01")]
  )

  station_data$Seasonal <- seasonal_component
  station_data$Adjusted <-
    station_data$Temperature - seasonal_component

  stopifnot(
    all(is.finite(station_data$Seasonal)),
    all(is.finite(station_data$Adjusted))
  )

  station_data
}

weather_adjusted <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    unname(station_ids),
    function(station_id) {
      adjust_weather_station(
        weather_data[
          weather_data$ID == station_id,
        ]
      )
    }
  )
)

rownames(weather_adjusted) <- NULL

weather_wide <- weather_adjusted |>
  dplyr::select(Date, Station, Adjusted) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Station,
    values_from = Adjusted
  ) |>
  arrange(Date)

weather_matrix <- as.matrix(
  weather_wide[, names(station_ids)]
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(weather_matrix) == length(weather_dates),
  ncol(weather_matrix) == 2L,
  all(is.finite(weather_matrix)),
  identical(
    as.numeric(weather_wide$Date),
    as.numeric(weather_dates)
  )
)

weather_adjusted_correlation <- cor(
  weather_matrix[, 1],
  weather_matrix[, 2]
)
```
```{r weather-seasonal-adjustment-plot, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=4.2, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Daily maximum temperatures at Houlton AP and Augusta State AP over 2022–2024, before and after seasonal adjustment. The seasonal components are estimated separately using the full 1988–2024 sample. Both panels retain all calendar days and use the same vertical scale."}
weather_plot_data <- weather_adjusted |>
  dplyr::filter(Date >= as.Date("2022-01-01")) |>
  dplyr::select(
    Date, Station, Temperature, Adjusted
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Temperature, Adjusted),
    names_to = "Series",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Series = factor(
      Series,
      levels = c("Temperature", "Adjusted"),
      labels = c(
        "A  Original temperatures",
        "B  Seasonally adjusted temperatures"
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(
  weather_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = Date,
    y = Value,
    color = Station
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~Series, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Houlton AP" = "#24476B",
      "Augusta State AP" = "#B36B35"
    ),
    breaks = names(station_ids),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 year",
    date_labels = "%Y",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  climate_theme +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#F2F2F2",
      color = NA
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(
      size = 9,
      hjust = 0
    ),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.8, "lines")
  )
```
The original series share a pronounced annual cycle,
with higher temperatures in summer and lower temperatures
in winter. After seasonal adjustment, this dominant pattern
is no longer apparent, while substantial daily fluctuations
remain and often occur together at the two stations.
Augusta also tends to retain a higher temperature level
than Houlton, since removing the seasonal component does
not remove differences in their average temperatures.

This visual association motivates modelling the two series
jointly, although it does not establish whether dependence
improves prediction. We next examine their contemporaneous
association and temporal persistence over the full
1988–2024 sample.
```{r weather-dependence-plot, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3.2, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Dependence in seasonally adjusted daily maximum temperatures over 1988–2024. Panel A shows contemporaneous observations at the two stations and a fitted linear regression line. Panel B shows sample autocorrelations at lags of 1–30 days, with approximate pointwise 95 percent white-noise reference bounds. These describe the adjusted temperature series, not model forecast errors."}
weather_scatter_data <- data.frame(
  Houlton = weather_matrix[, "Houlton AP"],
  Augusta = weather_matrix[, "Augusta State AP"]
)

weather_acf_data <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    seq_along(station_ids),
    function(j) {
      correlations <- as.numeric(
        stats::acf(
          weather_matrix[, j],
          lag.max = 30,
          plot = FALSE
        )$acf
      )[-1]

      data.frame(
        Lag = seq_along(correlations),
        ACF = correlations,
        Station = names(station_ids)[j]
      )
    }
  )
)

weather_acf_data$Station <- factor(
  weather_acf_data$Station,
  levels = names(station_ids)
)

weather_acf_bound <- qnorm(0.975) /
  sqrt(nrow(weather_matrix))

p_weather_scatter <- ggplot(

) +

  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +

p_weather_scatter + p_weather_acf +
  patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1))
```
After seasonal adjustment, the contemporaneous correlation
between the two stations is
`r sprintf("%.3f", weather_adjusted_correlation)`,
indicating substantial shared variation beyond the annual
temperature cycle. The scatter nevertheless shows dispersion
around the fitted line, so the stations retain distinct
daily movements.

Both series have similar autocorrelation patterns, with
a lag-one correlation of approximately 0.57 followed by
a rapid decline over the first few days. Smaller positive
correlations persist at longer lags, indicating that seasonal
adjustment leaves temporal dependence as well as cross-station
association. These features motivate the bivariate models
considered next, although contemporaneous correlation alone
does not establish a gain in one-day-ahead predictive accuracy.

# Bivariate Dynamic Linear Models

Let \(Y_t\) contain the seasonally adjusted maximum
temperatures at Houlton and Augusta, in that order.
We model their joint evolution through a bivariate
local-level specification:

\[
Y_t = \theta_t + v_t,
\qquad v_t \sim \mathcal{N}_2(0,V),
\]

\[
\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t,
\qquad w_t \sim \mathcal{N}_2(0,W).
\]

The latent vector \(\theta_t\) contains the two temperature
levels. Observation errors and state innovations are
independent over time, mutually independent, and independent
of the initial state. In all three specifications,
\(V=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{v,1}^2,\sigma_{v,2}^2)\),
so dependence between stations is introduced through
the evolution covariance \(W\).

Model 1 assumes independent level innovations:

\[
W_1 =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_{w,1}^2 & 0\\
0 & \sigma_{w,2}^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Together with the diagonal observation covariance and
independent initial states, this specification treats
the two stations as separate local-level models.
Model 2 instead estimates an unrestricted positive-definite
evolution covariance:

\[
W_2 =
\begin{pmatrix}
W_{11} & W_{12}\\
W_{12} & W_{22}
\end{pmatrix},
\]

allowing correlated innovations while retaining different
innovation variances at the two stations. Model 3 imposes
a distance-based structure:

\[
W_3 = \sigma_w^2
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \exp(-\phi d_{12})\\
\exp(-\phi d_{12}) & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \phi>0.
\]

Following the assignment, \(d_{12}\) is the Euclidean
distance between the stations' longitude–latitude coordinates,
measured in degrees. Model 3 therefore assumes equal
innovation variances and a positive correlation determined
by distance. With only two stations and one observed distance,
this specification allows a structured comparison with
Model 2, but cannot validate how dependence decays across
a wider geographical network.
```{r weather-model-definitions}
weather_coordinates <- weather_station_summary[
  match(
    names(station_ids),
    as.character(weather_station_summary$Station)
  ),
  c("Longitude", "Latitude")
]

weather_distance <- sqrt(
  sum(
    (
      as.numeric(unlist(weather_coordinates[1, ])) -
        as.numeric(unlist(weather_coordinates[2, ]))
    )^2
  )
)

stopifnot(
  is.finite(weather_distance),
  weather_distance > 0
)

make_weather_dlm <- function(V, W) {
  dlm::dlm(
    m0 = c(0, 0),
    C0 = diag(1e7, 2),
    FF = diag(2),
    V = V,
    GG = diag(2),
    W = W
  )
}

build_weather_m1 <- function(parameters) {
  V <- diag(exp(parameters[1:2]))
  W <- diag(exp(parameters[3:4]))

  make_weather_dlm(V, W)
}

build_weather_m2 <- function(parameters) {
  V <- diag(exp(parameters[1:2]))

  L <- matrix(
    c(
      exp(parameters[3]),
      parameters[4],
      0,
      exp(parameters[5])
    ),
    nrow = 2,
    ncol = 2
  )

  W <- tcrossprod(L)

  make_weather_dlm(V, W)
}

build_weather_m3 <- function(parameters) {
  V <- diag(exp(parameters[1:2]))

  innovation_variance <- exp(parameters[3])
  decay <- exp(parameters[4])
  correlation <- exp(-decay * weather_distance)

  W <- innovation_variance * matrix(
    c(1, correlation, correlation, 1),
    nrow = 2,
    ncol = 2
  )

  make_weather_dlm(V, W)
}
```
The models contain four, five, and four estimated covariance
parameters, respectively. We use logarithmic parameters
for positive quantities and a Cholesky factorization for
the unrestricted covariance in Model 2. All models share
a zero-mean Gaussian initial distribution with covariance
\(10^7 I_2\), used as a diffuse approximation, and are fitted
by maximizing the Gaussian Kalman-filter likelihood over
the same adjusted daily observations.

Optimization uses L-BFGS-B with broad numerical bounds
to prevent invalid or overflowing evaluations. Each
specification is fitted from three initial parameter vectors,
retaining the converged solution with the highest likelihood.
All retained solutions satisfy the optimizer's convergence
criterion and lie away from the imposed numerical bounds,
although these checks do not guarantee a global maximum.

For each model, all three initializations converged to
negative log-likelihood values differing by less than
\(4\times10^{-5}\), and none of the retained solutions
was near an imposed numerical bound.
```{r fit-weather-models, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list(weather_matrix, weather_distance, body(build_weather_m1), body(build_weather_m2), body(build_weather_m3), body(make_weather_dlm))}
weather_difference_variance <- apply(
  diff(weather_matrix),
  2,
  var
)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(weather_difference_variance)),
  all(weather_difference_variance > 0)
)

fit_weather_starts <- function(builder, starts) {
  n_parameters <- length(starts[[1]])

  lower_bounds <- rep(log(1e-8), n_parameters)
  upper_bounds <- rep(log(1e4), n_parameters)

  if (identical(builder, build_weather_m2)) {
    lower_bounds <- c(
      log(1e-8), log(1e-8),
      log(1e-4), -100, log(1e-4)
    )

    upper_bounds <- c(
      log(1e4), log(1e4),
      log(100), 100, log(100)
    )
  }

  objective <- function(parameters) {
    value <- tryCatch(
      dlm::dlmLL(
        y = weather_matrix,
        mod = builder(parameters)
      ),
      error = function(e) Inf
    )

    if (length(value) != 1L || !is.finite(value)) {
      return(1e50)
    }

    as.numeric(value)
  }

  attempts <- lapply(
    starts,
    function(initial_parameters) {
      tryCatch(
        stats::optim(
          par = initial_parameters,
          fn = objective,
          method = "L-BFGS-B",
          lower = lower_bounds,
          upper = upper_bounds,
          control = list(
            maxit = 2000,
            factr = 1e7
          )
        ),
        error = function(e) {
          list(
            convergence = NA_integer_,
            value = Inf,
            par = initial_parameters,
            message = conditionMessage(e)
          )
        }
      )
    }
  )

  successful <- vapply(
    attempts,
    function(result) {
      isTRUE(result$convergence == 0L) &&
        is.finite(result$value) &&
        result$value < 1e49 &&
        all(is.finite(result$par))
    },
    logical(1)
  )

  if (!any(successful)) {
    details <- vapply(
      attempts,
      function(result) {
        paste0(
          "convergence=", result$convergence,
          "; message=",
          paste(result$message, collapse = " ")
        )
      },
      character(1)
    )

    stop(
      "No converged fit for this weather model.\n",
      paste(details, collapse = "\n")
    )
  }

  successful_indices <- which(successful)

  best_index <- successful_indices[
    which.min(
      vapply(
        attempts[successful_indices],
        function(result) result$value,
        numeric(1)
      )
    )
  ]

  best_fit <- attempts[[best_index]]

  best_fit$lower_bounds <- lower_bounds
  best_fit$upper_bounds <- upper_bounds

  best_fit$near_numerical_bound <- any(
    abs(best_fit$par - lower_bounds) < 1e-4 |
      abs(best_fit$par - upper_bounds) < 1e-4
  )

  list(
    fit = best_fit,
    attempts = attempts
  )
}

weather_m1_starts <- lapply(
  c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75),
  function(observation_fraction) {
    log(
      c(
        observation_fraction *
          weather_difference_variance / 2,
        (1 - observation_fraction) *
          weather_difference_variance
      )
    )
  }
)

weather_m1_run <- fit_weather_starts(
  build_weather_m1,
  weather_m1_starts
)

weather_fit_m1 <- weather_m1_run$fit
weather_mod_m1 <- build_weather_m1(
  weather_fit_m1$par
)

weather_initial_v <- diag(weather_mod_m1$V)
weather_initial_w <- diag(weather_mod_m1$W)

weather_m2_starts <- lapply(
  c(0.30, 0.70, 0.95),
  function(initial_correlation) {
    c(
      log(weather_initial_v),
      log(sqrt(weather_initial_w[1])),
      initial_correlation *
        sqrt(weather_initial_w[2]),
      log(
        sqrt(
          weather_initial_w[2] *
            (1 - initial_correlation^2)
        )
      )
    )
  }
)

weather_m2_run <- fit_weather_starts(
  build_weather_m2,
  weather_m2_starts
)

weather_fit_m2 <- weather_m2_run$fit
weather_mod_m2 <- build_weather_m2(
  weather_fit_m2$par
)

weather_m3_starts <- lapply(
  c(0.30, 0.70, 0.95),
  function(initial_correlation) {
    initial_decay <- -log(initial_correlation) /
      weather_distance

    c(
      log(weather_initial_v),
      log(mean(weather_initial_w)),
      log(initial_decay)
    )
  }
)

weather_m3_run <- fit_weather_starts(
  build_weather_m3,
  weather_m3_starts
)

weather_fit_m3 <- weather_m3_run$fit
weather_mod_m3 <- build_weather_m3(
  weather_fit_m3$par
)

weather_fits <- list(
  M1 = weather_fit_m1,
  M2 = weather_fit_m2,
  M3 = weather_fit_m3
)

weather_models <- list(
  M1 = weather_mod_m1,
  M2 = weather_mod_m2,
  M3 = weather_mod_m3
)

stopifnot(
  all(
    vapply(
      weather_fits,
      function(result) {
        isTRUE(result$convergence == 0L) &&
          is.finite(result$value) &&
          result$value < 1e49
      },
      logical(1)
    )
  )
)

for (model in weather_models) {
  stopifnot(
    all(is.finite(model$V)),
    all(is.finite(model$W)),
    min(
      eigen(
        model$V,
        symmetric = TRUE,
        only.values = TRUE
      )$values
    ) > 0,
    min(
      eigen(
        model$W,
        symmetric = TRUE,
        only.values = TRUE
      )$values
    ) > 0
  )
}

weather_optimization_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = names(weather_fits),
  Convergence = vapply(
    weather_fits,
    function(result) as.integer(result$convergence),
    integer(1)
  ),
  Objective = vapply(
    weather_fits,
    function(result) result$value,
    numeric(1)
  ),
  NearNumericalBound = vapply(
    weather_fits,
    function(result) result$near_numerical_bound,
    logical(1)
  ),
  row.names = NULL
)
```
Approximate standard errors are calculated from the numerical
Hessian of the negative log-likelihood and transformed to
the reported parameter scale using the delta method.
They are omitted when the Hessian fails the numerical
conditioning check, when a fitted parameter is near an
imposed numerical bound, or when the absolute innovation
correlation is within \(10^{-6}\) of one.

All reported standard errors pass these checks, but remain
local approximations under the assumed Gaussian model,
conditional on the estimated seasonal adjustment.
Passing the numerical checks does not establish reliable
inference near a covariance boundary or protect against
misspecification of the temporal dynamics.
```{r weather-parameter-estimates}
weather_builders <- list(
  M1 = build_weather_m1,
  M2 = build_weather_m2,
  M3 = build_weather_m3
)

weather_parameter_values <- function(parameters, model_name) {
  model <- weather_builders[[model_name]](parameters)

  observation_variances <- diag(model$V)
  innovation_variances <- diag(model$W)

  innovation_correlation <- model$W[1, 2] /
    sqrt(prod(innovation_variances))

  if (model_name == "M1") {
    return(
      c(observation_variances, innovation_variances)
    )
  }

  if (model_name == "M2") {
    return(
      c(
        observation_variances,
        innovation_variances,
        model$W[1, 2],
        innovation_correlation
      )
    )
  }

  c(
    observation_variances,
    exp(parameters[3]),
    exp(parameters[4]),
    innovation_correlation
  )
}

weather_parameter_labels <- list(
  M1 = c(
    "Observation variance: Houlton",
    "Observation variance: Augusta",
    "Level innovation variance: Houlton",
    "Level innovation variance: Augusta"
  ),
  M2 = c(
    "Observation variance: Houlton",
    "Observation variance: Augusta",
    "Level innovation variance: Houlton",
    "Level innovation variance: Augusta",
    "Level innovation covariance",
    "Level innovation correlation"
  ),
  M3 = c(
    "Observation variance: Houlton",
    "Observation variance: Augusta",
    "Common level innovation variance",
    "Distance decay coefficient",
    "Level innovation correlation"
  )
)

weather_parameter_uncertainty <- function(model_name) {
  fitted <- weather_fits[[model_name]]
  parameters <- fitted$par
  builder <- weather_builders[[model_name]]

  estimates <- weather_parameter_values(
    parameters,
    model_name
  )

  standard_errors <- rep(
    NA_real_,
    length(estimates)
  )

  reason <- "Available"

  model <- builder(parameters)

  correlation <- model$W[1, 2] /
    sqrt(prod(diag(model$W)))

  if (isTRUE(fitted$near_numerical_bound)) {
    reason <- "Near numerical bound"
  } else if (1 - abs(correlation) < 1e-6) {
    reason <- "Near-boundary innovation correlation"
  } else {
    hessian <- tryCatch(
      stats::optimHess(
        par = parameters,
        fn = function(p) {
          dlm::dlmLL(
            y = weather_matrix,
            mod = builder(p)
          )
        }
      ),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (
      is.null(hessian) ||
      !all(is.finite(hessian))
    ) {
      reason <- "Hessian unavailable"
    } else {
      hessian <- (hessian + t(hessian)) / 2

      eigenvalues <- eigen(
        hessian,
        symmetric = TRUE,
        only.values = TRUE
      )$values

      if (
        min(eigenvalues) <=
          1e-8 * max(abs(eigenvalues))
      ) {
        reason <- "Hessian not sufficiently conditioned"
      } else {
        uncertainty <- tryCatch(
          {
            parameter_covariance <- solve(hessian)

            jacobian <- matrix(
              NA_real_,
              nrow = length(estimates),
              ncol = length(parameters)
            )

            for (j in seq_along(parameters)) {
              step <- 1e-5 * max(
                1,
                abs(parameters[j])
              )

              upper <- lower <- parameters
              upper[j] <- upper[j] + step
              lower[j] <- lower[j] - step

              jacobian[, j] <- (
                weather_parameter_values(
                  upper,
                  model_name
                ) -
                  weather_parameter_values(
                    lower,
                    model_name
                  )
              ) / (2 * step)
            }

            reported_covariance <- jacobian %*%
              parameter_covariance %*%
              t(jacobian)

            reported_variances <- diag(
              reported_covariance
            )

            if (
              !all(is.finite(reported_variances)) ||
              any(reported_variances < 0)
            ) {
              stop("Invalid delta-method variances")
            }

            sqrt(reported_variances)
          },
          error = function(e) NULL
        )

        if (is.null(uncertainty)) {
          reason <- "Covariance calculation unavailable"
        } else {
          standard_errors <- uncertainty
        }
      }
    }
  }

  list(
    table = data.frame(
      Model = model_name,
      Parameter = weather_parameter_labels[[model_name]],
      Estimate = as.numeric(estimates),
      SE = standard_errors
    ),
    reason = reason
  )
}

weather_uncertainty <- lapply(
  names(weather_fits),
  weather_parameter_uncertainty
)

names(weather_uncertainty) <- names(weather_fits)

weather_parameter_table <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    weather_uncertainty,
    function(result) result$table
  )
)

rownames(weather_parameter_table) <- NULL

weather_se_status <- data.frame(
  Model = names(weather_uncertainty),
  Status = vapply(
    weather_uncertainty,
    function(result) result$reason,
    character(1)
  ),
  row.names = NULL
)

format_weather_parameter <- function(value) {
  if (!is.finite(value)) {
    return("Not reported")
  }

  if (value != 0 && abs(value) < 0.001) {
    return(formatC(value, format = "e", digits = 3))
  }

  formatC(value, format = "f", digits = 4)
}

weather_parameter_display <- weather_parameter_table

weather_parameter_display$Estimate <- vapply(
  weather_parameter_table$Estimate,
  format_weather_parameter,
  character(1)
)

weather_parameter_display$SE <- vapply(
  weather_parameter_table$SE,
  format_weather_parameter,
  character(1)
)
correlation_rows <- weather_parameter_table$Parameter ==
  "Level innovation correlation"

weather_parameter_display$Estimate[correlation_rows] <-
  formatC(
    weather_parameter_table$Estimate[correlation_rows],
    format = "f",
    digits = 6
  )

  weather_parameter_display,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "Model", "Parameter", "Estimate", "Approx. SE"
  ),
  caption = paste(
    "Maximum-likelihood covariance parameter estimates.",
    "Variances and covariances are in squared degrees Celsius;",
